Decompositions#

Decomposition algorithms approximate tensors and functions as tensor trains (TT), tensor rings (TR), or their matrix and Quantics extensions. The usual workflow is to describe the input with a source, construct a decomposition engine, and call its fit method. Optional strategy objects configure steps such as sampling, local optimization and convergence.

import torch
import tensorkrowch as tk

d = tk.decompositions
source = d.DenseTensorSource(torch.randn(4, 5, 6, 4))
engine = d.TTSVD(source)
result = engine.fit(rank=4)
approximation = result.contract_dense()

Results are numerical Formats with additional fit diagnostics. A TT has open boundaries; a TR connects the first and last core with a cyclic bond. Both are supported throughout the guide.

Choosing a method#

Approach

Input and intended use

Tensor train

Tensor ring

SVD

A finite tensor that fits in memory; successive matrix factorizations.

TTSVD

TRSVD

Alternating least squares

Fit chosen ranks by optimizing cores, using all entries or sampled rows.

TTALS

TRALS

Recursive sketching from samples

An evaluable source and configurations defining the region of interest.

TTRSS

TRRSS

Recursive sketching with operators

A finite source and selected fibers, marginalizations or TT sketches.

TTRS

Apply TT2TR to the resulting TT if needed.

Conversion and spectral recovery

Convert an existing TT, or recover an exact TR by spectral methods.

The TT is the input to conversion.

TT2TR, tr_blostr(), tr_blostr_svd()

The examples use engine objects. Functions such as tt_svd(), tr_als() and tt_rss() provide shorter interfaces for a single fit. The Decomposition API reference lists their complete signatures and all configurable components.

Describing the input#

A source separates how values are obtained from how they are decomposed. Choose one of the following BaseSource implementations:

Source

Use it for

DenseTensorSource

A PyTorch tensor with one axis per variable.

SparseTensorSource

Indexed entries of a finite tensor; unstored entries are zero.

FormatSource

An existing tensor format, TT cores, or an MPS/MPO model.

CallableTensorSource

A function of finite discrete indices, with explicit input dimensions.

CallableSource

A function of continuous inputs, for sampled sketching with embeddings.

CallableQuanticsSource

A coordinate function discretized into digit sites on a Quantics grid.

For example, a discrete callable evaluates a batch of index configurations:

def function(indices):
    return (indices.to(torch.float64) + 1).prod(dim=1)

source = d.CallableTensorSource(function, in_dim=(4, 4, 4, 4))
engine = d.TTSVD(source)
result = engine.fit(rank=2)

Sources expose BaseSource.evaluate() for configurations, BaseSource.fiber() to vary one input, and BaseSource.contract_dense() to materialize a finite tensor. Configuration columns follow in_sites; ConfigurationBatch can explicitly group index or feature inputs. Vector sources use in_sites to select evaluated variables; unselected axes remain open in the output.

Dense tensors can also be passed directly to engines that accept them. as_tensor_source() provides the corresponding adaptation explicitly. SVD materializes even sparse or callable sources; ALS and sampled sketching can query their entries without constructing the complete tensor.

Dataset constructors#

Use SparseTensorSource.from_data for discrete empirical masses. CallableSource.from_data describes continuous data, optionally smoothed with a kernel. CallableTensorSource.from_data and CallableQuanticsSource.from_data provide the corresponding finite and quantized constructions. For example:

dataset = torch.rand(64, 3)
source = d.CallableSource.from_data(
    dataset, kernel=d.gaussian_kernel, bandwidth=0.2)

gaussian_kernel() also works independently on query coordinates and kernel centers. See each from_data method for weights and domain options.

SVD decompositions#

SVD methods factor a finite tensor into smaller cores. They provide direct decompositions without iterative core optimization. The engine materializes the source at construction; repeated fits reuse that prepared tensor.

TT-SVD#

TTSVD applies successive truncated SVDs along an open chain, following Oseledets’ tensor train construction [ttsvd].

axis = torch.arange(1, 5, dtype=torch.float64)
tensor = torch.einsum('i,j,k,l->ijkl', axis, axis, axis, axis) + 1
source = d.DenseTensorSource(tensor)
engine = d.TTSVD(source)
result = engine.fit(rank=2, collect_metrics=True)
approximation = result.contract_dense()

rank is an upper bound at each cut. cutoff, atol, rtol and cum_percentage select singular values according to truncated_svd(). In particular, SVD rtol limits the discarded squared singular-value mass relative to the total squared mass; it is not a relative residual stopping criterion. Multiple criteria use the most restrictive retained rank.

TT-SVD accepts a shared integer rank cap. It supports leading structural batches declared through DenseTensorSource(..., n_batches=...).

TR-SVD#

TRSVD constructs a cyclic chain, based on the TR-SVD approach of Zhao et al. [trdecomp]. This implementation starts with an interior bipartition and decomposes the two resulting subchains, rather than using the original one-direction construction.

axis = torch.arange(1, 5, dtype=torch.float64)
tensor = torch.einsum('i,j,k,l->ijkl', axis, axis, axis, axis) + 1
source = d.DenseTensorSource(tensor)
engine = d.TRSVD(source, center=2)
result = engine.fit(rank=2, collect_metrics=True)
approximation = result.contract_dense()

Here center specifies the cut between sites center - 1 and center. An integer rank caps every TR bond, including the cyclic bond; its square caps the initial matrix rank. The initial retained dimension is factored into two TR dimensions. Any structural zero padding needed for that factorization is recorded in metadata.

The singular-value criteria are the same as in TT-SVD. TR-SVD does not support structural batches, and its local truncation diagnostics are not a global reconstruction bound.

Repeated fits and numerical options#

Both engines allow independent fits with different truncation controls:

source = d.DenseTensorSource(torch.eye(4, dtype=torch.float64))
engine = d.TTSVD(source)
rank_one = engine.fit(rank=1)
rank_two = engine.fit(rank=2)

renormalize controls numerical scaling, and out_device selects where final cores are stored. The exact SVD backend is configured through set_svd_method() or svd_method(). These methods need no extra strategy object for ordinary truncation. Matrix engines are TTMSVD and TRMSVD; input preparation is described below.

Alternating least squares#

ALS optimizes one core while holding the others fixed, then visits the next site. Use it to fit prescribed ranks, refine an existing approximation, or fit selected observations. Unlike a direct SVD, an ALS fit depends on its initialization and stopping criteria.

TT-ALS#

TTALS uses alternating forward and reverse passes over an open chain. This is the one-core alternating linear scheme underlying TT optimization [ttals]; it does not implement two-core MALS rank adaptation.

axis = torch.arange(1, 5, dtype=torch.float64)
tensor = torch.einsum('i,j,k,l->ijkl', axis, axis, axis, axis) + 1
source = d.DenseTensorSource(tensor)
engine = d.TTALS(source)
convergence = d.ConvergencePolicy(max_sweeps=30, rtol=1e-8)
result = engine.fit(rank=2, convergence=convergence)

Without initial_cores, initialization is random. To refine another fit, pass its result or cores as initial_cores; an SVD initialization is an explicit composition with TTSVD. fixed_cores freezes selected cores. The default gauge="qr" moves the orthogonality center between updates; gauge="none" replaces cores without that QR preparation.

A rank sequence has one entry per open-chain bond, so a four-site TT uses three entries. Each directional pass counts as one sweep.

TR-ALS#

TRALS optimizes a cyclic chain using forward passes. Its cyclic least-squares formulation follows the tensor ring approach [trdecomp]. Initialization, conditioning and convergence can differ from TT-ALS because every core participates in a closed loop.

cores = [torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(5)]
source = d.FormatSource(tk.formats.TR(cores))
engine = d.TRALS(source)
convergence = d.ConvergencePolicy(
    max_sweeps=30, rtol=1e-8, keep_best=True)
result = engine.fit(rank=2, convergence=convergence)

A TR rank sequence has one right-link rank per core. Its last entry is the cyclic rank, so a five-site TR uses five entries. QR is a local gauge transfer in a ring; it does not make the whole cyclic environment orthonormal.

Configuring convergence and local solves#

The same objects configure both engines:

  • ConvergencePolicy sets the sweep budget, absolute and relative objective-error thresholds, stagnation criteria, and optional retention of the best complete-sweep approximation. A stagnation threshold indicates little change, not necessarily a small reconstruction error.

  • LeastSquaresSolver configures the PyTorch least-squares solve, conditioning controls and optional Tikhonov regularization.

  • SamplingPolicy replaces complete local systems with sampled rows. The next section lists its sampling choices.

For example, a regularized refinement can reuse a previous result:

source = d.DenseTensorSource(torch.ones(3, 4, 3, dtype=torch.float64))
initial = d.TTSVD(source).fit(rank=2)
engine = d.TTALS(source)
solver = d.LeastSquaresSolver(l2_reg=1e-10)
convergence = d.ConvergencePolicy(
    max_sweeps=20, stagnation_rtol=1e-8, patience=3, keep_best=True)
result = engine.fit(
    initial_cores=initial, solver=solver, convergence=convergence)

Sampling and partial observations#

Pass a SamplingPolicy to fit when local systems should use a subset of rows. The policy selects topology-specific samplers internally:

Policy method

TT

TR

"uniform"

UniformRows

UniformRows

"leverage"

TTLeverageRows, using mixed-canonical cores [ttleverage].

TRProductLeverageRows, using a product proposal [trproduct].

"exact_leverage"

Not available.

TRExactLeverageRows, using cyclic Gram contractions [trexact].

 
source = d.DenseTensorSource(torch.ones(4, 4, 4, 4, dtype=torch.float64))
engine = d.TTALS(source)
sampler = d.SamplingPolicy(n_samples=64, method='leverage')
convergence = d.ConvergencePolicy(
    max_sweeps=20, rtol=1e-8, error_samples=128)
result = engine.fit(
    rank=2, sampler=sampler, convergence=convergence,
    collect_metrics=True)

Sampled least-squares rows are corrected using their proposal probabilities. reuse_sweeps controls reuse of uniform samples; leverage proposals depend on the current site and cores. TR leverage methods retain complete active physical fibers, so n_samples counts exterior configurations rather than scalar rows.

Stopping errors are measured on a separate fixed uniform evaluation set, not on each changing training sample. ConvergencePolicy.error_samples sets its budget; None requests exact evaluation. Estimated measurements are identified in result.metadata['error_evaluation'].

For missing data, pass a boolean mask to the engine constructor: true entries participate, including observed zeros. weights separately multiplies participating residuals before their squared norm is taken. An ordinary sparse source still represents known zeros outside its support; it is not automatically a completion dataset. ALSProblem describes these objective distinctions, and ObservedRows exposes permanent sparse observations for lower-level use. Neither is required for ordinary engine fits.

TT to TR conversion and spectral recovery#

The ring module converts an existing TT to a cyclic representation. It also provides local loop-opening strategies, reused by TR-RSS. The optimization route combines local TR-ALS with recursive gauge transport; the spectral route uses BLOSTR [blostr]. The recursive enrichment and automatic block handling are implementation extensions, not guarantees from the BLOSTR paper.

Converting an existing TT#

TT2TR takes a TT rather than a source. When starting from values, first obtain that TT using a source and another decomposition:

axis = torch.arange(1, 5, dtype=torch.float64)
tensor = torch.einsum('i,j,k,l->ijkl', axis, axis, axis, axis) + 1
source = d.DenseTensorSource(tensor)
initial_tt = d.TTSVD(source).fit(rank=4)
converter = d.TT2TR(initial_tt)
result = converter.fit(rank=2, collect_metrics=True)

An integer rank specifies the local TR ranks; a sequence gives one right-link rank per core, with the cyclic rank last. Omitting it requests rank discovery. The initial site grows into a block when necessary to expose sufficient physical dimensions. block_boundaries controls automatic end blocks; disabling it for optimization requires prescribed ranks.

center selects the initial site or the center of the discovery block. At block SVD splits, rank acts as a cap and an optional rtol can reduce the returned ranks. This tolerance controls discarded squared singular-value mass, not ALS convergence.

Choosing a loop opener#

A loop opener factors a local target into TR cores and two external gauges. Choose a strategy to control that factorization:

Object

Role

ALSLoopOpener

Optimize the local factors. Its fit_options accepts TR-ALS controls such as a solver and convergence policy.

QRLoopOpener

Balance an opening with QR, use another opener, restore the factors and optionally refine in the original target coordinates.

BLOSTRLoopOpener

Recover all local factors using the spectral BLOSTR algorithm.

BLOSTRSVDLoopOpener

Recover the first spectral factor, then split the remainder by SVD.

CallableLoopOpener

Supply a custom implementation of the LoopOpener contract.

The strings "als", "blostr" and "blostr_svd" select the corresponding built-in strategies with default settings. Use objects when their detailed options are needed. LoopOpening documents the returned local factors; ordinary conversion code need not construct it.

For a conversion with customized local optimization, pass a configured opener. This example also balances each target and refines its factors:

cores = [torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(5)]
source = d.FormatSource(tk.formats.TR(cores))
initial_tt = d.TTSVD(source).fit(rank=4)
convergence = d.ConvergencePolicy(
    max_sweeps=50, rtol=1e-10, keep_best=True)
opener = d.QRLoopOpener(d.ALSLoopOpener({
    'convergence': convergence,
}))
converter = d.TT2TR(initial_tt)
result = converter.fit(rank=2, loop_opener=opener, enrich=True)

Recursion and enrichment#

Optimization openings are connected using a gauge recursion. The supported choices are:

  • "adjoint" / AdjointGaugeRecursion: move QR centers, or use the corresponding isometries of a Vidal representation. This is the default.

  • "pinv" / PinvGaugeRecursion: use pseudoinverses of local TT cores or contracted blocks.

  • "orth" / OrthGaugeRecursion: use pseudoinverses of the learned gauges.

A configured GaugeRecursion strategy accepts PyTorch pseudoinverse keyword arguments. enrich=True adds orthogonal residual constraints to the transported sample space without increasing the requested TR ranks. enrich_rank and enrich_rtol limit those extra coordinates.

Exact spectral recovery#

BLOSTR is intended for exact spectral structure under its dimensional and genericity assumptions [blostr]. Choosing a BLOSTR opener in TT2TR selects an exact propagation route: recover the central factors, absorb square gauges into neighbors and continue with SVDs. It does not use the optimization gauge recursions or enrichment.

The standalone functions tr_blostr() and tr_blostr_svd() instead take a dense tensor and return a TR decomposition directly. Their API documents rank discovery, slice selection and Gaussian projection options. The Gaussian projection and first-factor/SVD variant are extensions of the basic spectral construction. Arbitrary noisy inputs need not satisfy the requirements for exact recovery.

For an exact generic TR input, the first-factor/SVD route can be selected explicitly. BLOSTR uses complex spectral factors and automatically promotes the working TT cores, so real inputs are accepted and the result is complex. The input TT remains unchanged:

cores = [torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(5)]
source = d.FormatSource(tk.formats.TR(cores))
initial_tt = d.TTSVD(source).fit(rank=4)
opener = d.BLOSTRSVDLoopOpener({
    'projection': 'gaussian', 'n_attempts': 4,
})
converter = d.TT2TR(initial_tt)
result = converter.fit(rank=2, loop_opener=opener, rtol=1e-8)

Recursive sketching#

Sketching builds smaller local tensors from evaluations or contractions, then connects their factors. It avoids materializing the complete target. TT-RSS and TR-RSS share sampled preparation; TT-RS uses explicitly selected contraction operators. These methods do not support structural batches.

TT-RSS: a tensor train from evaluations#

TTRSS implements Tensor Train Recursive Sketching from Samples [ttrss]. The source must be evaluable at new configurations: supplied samples determine the sketches, rather than restricting queries to those original points.

def function(coordinates):
    return (1 + coordinates).prod(dim=1)

source = d.CallableSource(function, n_sites=4, dtype=torch.float64)
domain = torch.linspace(0, 1, 8, dtype=torch.float64)
samples = torch.rand(128, 4, dtype=torch.float64)

def embedding(values):
    return torch.stack((torch.ones_like(values), values), dim=-1)

engine = d.TTRSS(source, embedding=embedding, domain=domain)
result = engine.fit(samples, rank=2, center=1, collect_metrics=True)
embedded = embedding(samples)
values = result.evaluate(embedded)

Continuous inputs need an embedding and a domain on which its coefficients can be fitted. A shared embedding/domain applies to every input; sequences allow different choices per input. Finite tensor sources use basis embeddings by default, so they need neither argument.

rank caps TT bonds; None discovers numerical ranks. center is a site: local SVDs act on both sides there and on the outgoing side elsewhere. Singular spectra remain absorbed in the prepared tensors. batch_size limits source-evaluation batches, not the number of sketch samples.

TR-RSS: a tensor ring from evaluations#

TRRSS uses the same source, samples, embeddings and transformations, but constructs a cyclic representation through local loop openings. It is an experimental extension combining TT-RSS [ttrss] with the ring opening machinery described above; it is not the TT algorithm with a final unit-rank closing bond.

cores = [torch.randn(2, 4, 2, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(5)]
source = d.FormatSource(tk.formats.TR(cores))
samples = torch.randint(4, (128, 5))
engine = d.TRRSS(source)
result = engine.fit(samples, rank=2, collect_metrics=True)

The rank sequence has one right-link rank per final core, with the cyclic rank last. Sampled TT-cut caps are formed from products of cyclic and internal TR ranks. With no prescribed rank, local SVDs and blocks determine the numerical dimensions used for discovery.

center seeds an automatic initial block. End blocks absorb the incoming gauges before being split; block_boundaries=False keeps single-site ends when ranks are prescribed. The block and rank conventions follow TT2TR. Recursive steps transport gauges through sketch evaluations, retaining the inherited sample coordinates. Local ALS stopping criteria belong to the opener’s convergence policy, while fit truncation criteria control SVDs. Pass a configured ALSLoopOpener to customize those solves, or wrap it in QRLoopOpener for balancing and refinement as in the conversion example.

Choosing fitters and projectors#

Both sampled engines accept strategy objects in their constructors:

Object

When to use it

BasisFitter

Represent a finite physical axis in its discrete basis.

FixedEmbeddingFitter

Fit coefficients in a supplied embedding, with optional solver settings.

TrainableEmbeddingFitter

Optimize a parameterized embedding while fitting physical fibers.

IdentityRangeProjector

Apply the local SVD directly; this is also the default when omitted.

RandomizedRangeProjector

Compress the local SVD input using a configured randomized projection.

Pass a fitter through input_fitter and a projector through range_projector. InputFitter and RangeProjector document the extension contracts. local_solver configures the linear solves used to align the TT cores; it is separate from a TR loop opener’s ALS solver.

source = d.DenseTensorSource(torch.ones(4, 4, 4, 4, dtype=torch.float64))
samples = torch.randint(4, (64, 4))
projector = d.RandomizedRangeProjector(
    projection_dim=4, projection_oversampling=2, n_power_iter=1)
engine = d.TTRSS(source, range_projector=projector)
result = engine.fit(samples, rank=2)

Transforming evaluations#

For TT-RSS and TR-RSS, transform is one callback on a shared ConfigurationMap. It receives query configurations and raw source values, and returns transformed values of the same shape. Its evaluate method queries additional points through the cache without increasing the sketch sample set. For example, a reflection average is:

def function(coordinates):
    return (1 + coordinates).prod(dim=1)

def transform(configuration_map):
    reflected = 1 - configuration_map.configurations
    return (configuration_map.values +
            configuration_map.evaluate(reflected)) / 2

source = d.CallableSource(function, n_sites=3, dtype=torch.float64)
domain = torch.linspace(0, 1, 8, dtype=torch.float64)
samples = torch.rand(64, 3, dtype=torch.float64)

def embedding(values):
    return torch.stack((torch.ones_like(values), values), dim=-1)

engine = d.TTRSS(
    source, embedding=embedding, domain=domain, transform=transform)
result = engine.fit(samples, rank=2)

Tensor-valued functions#

A callable can return output axes as well as its configuration batch. Declare them through the source’s out_shape and select the input variables with in_sites; n_sites counts both input and output variables. out_position places the output sites in the fitted chain. labels optionally selects output components for building the sample sketches.

def function(coordinates):
    value = coordinates.sum(dim=1)
    return torch.stack((value, value.square()), dim=1)

def embedding(values):
    return torch.stack((torch.ones_like(values), values,
                        values.square()), dim=-1)

source = d.CallableSource(
    function, n_sites=4, out_shape=(2,), dtype=torch.float64,
    in_sites=(0, 1, 2))
engine = d.TTRSS(
    source, embedding=embedding,
    domain=torch.linspace(0, 1, 8, dtype=torch.float64), out_position=1)
samples = torch.rand(64, 3, dtype=torch.float64)
labels = torch.arange(64).remainder(2)
result = engine.fit(samples, labels=labels, rank=4)

TT-RS: explicit contraction sketches#

TTRS builds local core-determining equations from a finite source and a SketchOperator, following tensor train sketching [ttrs]. Its finite-source interface also permits exact contractions rather than only empirical estimates from observations. Centered construction and the available operators extend that basic formulation.

dataset = torch.randint(4, (128, 4))
source = d.SparseTensorSource.from_data(dataset, in_dim=(4, 4, 4, 4))
sketch = d.MarginalSketch(order=1)
engine = d.TTRS(source, sketch_operator=sketch)
result = engine.fit(rank=2, collect_metrics=True)

Available contraction strategies are:

  • SampledSketch: select fibers using supplied or generated indices.

  • MarginalSketch: form local marginals, with configurable order and optional per-site factors. This is the default strategy.

  • TTStackSketch: contract a stack of TT sketches; its construction is related to randomized TT sketching [ttstack].

Here transform acts separately on each three-axis Phi tensor, returning a tensor of the same shape. This allows local smoothing or other user-defined operations on the projected tensors. It differs from the shared evaluation callback used by RSS. The callback is responsible for preserving whatever consistency its application requires.

center, SVD truncation and range_projector work as in the other sketching engines. strict_system enables additional checks on the core-determining equations. PhiOperator and CoreDeterminingSystem document lower-level access for custom sketches. There is no separate TR-RS wrapper: compose the resulting TT with TT2TR when needed.

Matrix and Quantics extensions#

These extensions describe the input and result representation; the numerical algorithms and their configurable strategies remain the same.

Matrices#

A matrix source has paired input/output dimensions at every site. Dense, sparse and callable sources provide .matrix(...) constructors; FormatSource reads those dimensions from a matrix format.

# Two input axes followed by two output axes.
tensor = torch.randn(3, 4, 3, 4, dtype=torch.float64)
source = d.DenseTensorSource.matrix(tensor, ordering='grouped')
tt_engine = d.TTMSVD(source)
tr_engine = d.TRMSVD(source)
ttm = tt_engine.fit(rank=4)
trm = tr_engine.fit(rank=4)

ordering="grouped" means (in_0, in_1, ..., out_0, out_1, ...); "interleaved" means (in_0, out_0, in_1, out_1, ...). An ordinary two-axis matrix is one paired site; reshape it first to specify more sites. Sparse matrix sources additionally need in_dim and out_dim.

General engines such as TTALS, TRALS, TTRSS and TRRSS infer matrix results from the source. They return TTMDecomposition or TRMDecomposition, with each physical input/output pair restored. TTMSVD and TRMSVD explicitly require matrix inputs. Matrix apply and contraction behavior follow the corresponding formats.

Quantics#

Quantics sources discretize coordinate functions into digit sites. Construct the source with base, level and domain or explicit grid_coordinates. A preconfigured QuantizedLayout and CoordinateMap can express more detailed layouts and grids. These digit representations follow the Quantics construction [quantics].

def function(coordinates):
    return torch.exp(coordinates.sum(dim=1))

source = d.CallableQuanticsSource(
    function, n_coordinates=2, base=2, level=(3, 4),
    domain=torch.tensor([[0., 1.], [-1., 1.]], dtype=torch.float64),
    dtype=torch.float64)
tt_engine = d.TTSVD(source)
tr_engine = d.TRSVD(source)
qtt = tt_engine.fit(rank=2)
qtr = tr_engine.fit(rank=2)
coordinates = torch.tensor([[0., -1.], [0.5, 0.]], dtype=torch.float64)
values = qtt.evaluate_coordinates(coordinates)

The results are QTTDecomposition or QTRDecomposition; matrix sources yield QTTMDecomposition or QTRMDecomposition. Results retain their digit layouts and coordinate maps. SVD materializes the full digit tensor, while ALS and RSS can query it.

Sampled sketching accepts domain-coordinate samples for Quantics sources. An explicit ConfigurationBatch(..., kind="indices") supplies digit indices instead. The layout can group digits by variable or interleave them by level. Functions qtt_svd(), qtr_svd(), qttm_svd(), qtrm_svd(), qtt_rss() and qtr_rss() are convenient adapters, not separate numerical engines. Ordinary dense tensors are not automatically quantized.

Results, progress and diagnostics#

Every decomposition returns a TensorDecomposition together with the appropriate numerical format interface. Use result.cores to access its cores, evaluate for selected inputs, and contract_dense when full materialization is affordable. Continuous RSS results are evaluated on embedded inputs, as shown above; Quantics results also support coordinate evaluation.

verbose controls console progress. collect_metrics=True retains algorithm-specific records in DecompositionMetrics: truncations, local solves, sweep errors, evaluations and timings. See each fit method for its reporting levels. A small local opening or sampled solve residual does not by itself certify a small global reconstruction error.

result.as_info() combines representation information and diagnostics. result.metadata records the fit setup. These describe the original fit; editing or rounding the result does not recompute historical errors. result.error(...) can measure the current approximation on supplied data. result.to_format() returns the numerical representation without fit diagnostics. Copying, detaching and moving results preserve their history; new algebraic operations return ordinary formats.

The legacy vec_to_mps() and mat_to_mpo() remain available for compatibility and emit deprecation warnings. New code should use the engine or functional decomposition interfaces and construct models explicitly.
